bib.title: Data Selection for Language Models via Importance Resampling

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed only for lineage; quality-filter example text in Appendix J not examined in detail.

question: How can a pretraining subset be selected cheaply from a huge raw text corpus so that it matches a desired target distribution, and does that improve downstream performance?
hypothesis: Importance resampling in a reduced hashed n-gram feature space selects data closer to the target than heuristic classification or random selection, and the closeness (KL reduction) predicts downstream accuracy.
contributions: DSIR: importance resampling on a hashed n-gram feature space, selecting 100M Pile documents in 4.5 hours
KL reduction data metric that correlates with downstream accuracy (r=0.82) across 8 selection methods
DSIR matches expert curation for domain-specific continued pretraining and beats random and heuristic filtering by 2-2.5% on GLUE for general-domain pretraining

method.summary: DSIR hashes unigrams and bigrams into 10k buckets, fits bag-of-n-grams generative models to raw (Pile) and target data by counting, computes importance weights p_hat/q_hat per raw example, and samples k examples without replacement with the Gumbel top-k trick. It is compared with random selection, GPT-3-style heuristic classification, top-k variants and DAPT manual curation in continued pretraining (RoBERTa-base, 8 tasks) and from-scratch BERT-base pretraining (GLUE).
method.task: pretraining data selection (masked language modelling), evaluated by fine-tuning

datasets.name: The Pile
datasets.size: 1.6B examples (intro); 1.7B examples of 128 whitespace words (Appendix F)
datasets.split: chunk 0 reserved for validation, last 29 of 30 chunks used
datasets.preprocessing: split into 128-word examples; quality filter for heuristic classification and DSIR: word length 40-500, repeat ratio 0.02-0.2, informativeness ratio 0.3-0.7, numeric ratio <0.2 (52% of examples kept); random selection uses unfiltered Pile

datasets.name: 8 downstream tasks (ACL-ARC, Sci-ERC, ChemProt, RCT, HyperPartisan, AGNews, Helpfulness, IMDB)
datasets.split: unlabeled training inputs used as DSIR target; fine-tuned on the task

datasets.name: Wikipedia + books (Books3, BookCorpus2, Gutenberg) from Pile validation set
GLUE (MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST-2, MRPC, CoLA, STS-B)

models.name: BERT-base (trained from scratch on selected data)

training.lr: from scratch: 1e-3 (8e-4 for DSIR, since 1e-3 diverged); continued pretraining RoBERTa: 5e-4 or 1e-4 (1e-4 if 5e-4 diverged); BERT continued: 1e-4
training.warmup: from scratch 3000 steps; RoBERTa continued 720 steps; BERT continued 1440 steps
training.batch_size: from scratch 4096 (16 accumulation steps on 4 GPUs); RoBERTa continued 4096; BERT continued 2048
training.steps: from scratch 50000; RoBERTa continued 12500; BERT continued 25000
training.epochs: inferred: 4 epochs over 51.2M selected examples for from-scratch runs (stated in Section 7)
training.tokens: 26B tokens processed from scratch (128 x 4096 x 50000); BERT continued adds 26B to BERT's 43B for 69B total
training.seq_len: 128 from scratch; 256 RoBERTa continued; 512 BERT continued
training.compute: about 50 hours per from-scratch run; about 60 hours per BERT continued pretraining run

other.domain_specific_compute: equal token budget to DAPT models of Gururangan et al. 2020; 25M selected examples of fixed token length 256
other.general_domain_selection: 51.2M examples selected (102.4M then concatenated in pairs); 96% from non-Wikipedia/books domains, 4% uniform from Wikipedia and books
other.glue_finetune: 10 epochs, batch 32 or 16, lr 1e-5 or 2e-5, AdamW weight decay 0.1, betas 0.9/0.98, eps 1e-6, warmup ratio 0.06, polynomial schedule, FP16; RTE, MRPC, STS-B start from MNLI model
other.domain_finetune: batch size 4096 listed in Table 11, 3 or 10 epochs chosen on validation over 5 seeds, patience 3, max length 256 (512 for reviews and for DAPT)

parameters.ngrams: unigrams and bigrams hashed into the same space
parameters.resampling: k samples without replacement via Gumbel top-k
parameters.heuristic_classification: fasttext bigram classifier, 2M hash tokens, 300-d pretrained subword vectors, autotune 30 min, Pareto shape 9
parameters.neural_variant: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 384-d embeddings, GMMs with 1000 (raw) and 50 (target) components, diagonal covariance

metrics.name: macro-F1 (micro-F1 for ChemProt and RCT)
metrics.definition: downstream fine-tuning F1 on 8 tasks, averaged over 5 seeds

metrics.name: KL reduction
metrics.definition: mean over targets of KL(target||raw) minus KL(target||selected) on hashed n-gram distributions, estimated from first 100k examples of each dataset

baselines: manual curation / DAPT checkpoints (Gururangan et al. 2020)
eval.protocol: 5 seeds, standard deviations reported in tables; no significance tests; one selection run per method.

evidence.quote: hash each n-grams into one of m buckets (m = 10000 in this paper)

results.claim: DSIR selects 100M documents from the full Pile in 4.5 hours on one 96-core CPU node.
results.setup: hashed n-gram DSIR, 10k buckets, raw distribution fit with 1B hashed indices, target ChemProt, 1 CPU node with 96 cores, no preprocessing other than decompression
results.quote: DSIR selects 100M documents from the full Pile dataset in 4.5 hours on 1 CPU node with 96 cores.
results.note: 4.36 hours of the total is computing importance weights; fitting 1 minute, resampling 6 minutes

results.claim: General-domain BERT-base trained from scratch on DSIR-selected data reaches 82.30 average GLUE dev accuracy, versus 80.25 for random selection.
results.setup: target is Wikipedia + books (Pile validation set); 51.2M examples selected from the Pile; BERT-base, 50k steps, batch 4096, length 128; heuristic classification 79.85, top-k heuristic 81.47, top-k DSIR 81.38
results.quote: DSIR achieves 82.3% average GLUE accuracy, improving over random selection by 2% and heuristic classification by 2.5%.
results.table: Table 3, row DSIR / Random selection, column Avg (82.30 / 80.25)

results.claim: In domain-specific continued pretraining from RoBERTa-base, DSIR averages 83.76 F1 over 8 tasks versus 83.46 for DAPT manual curation and 82.58 for random selection.
results.setup: RoBERTa-base start; 25M selected Pile examples per task, length 256, same token compute for all methods; target is each task's unlabeled inputs; RoBERTa no continued pretraining 82.20; heuristic classification 82.88; top-k heuristic 83.65
results.quote: On average, DSIR improves over random selection by 1.2% and manually curated data (DAPT) by 0.3%, showing the potential to replace manual curation.
results.table: Table 1, row DSIR / Manual curation/DAPT / Random selection, column Avg (83.76 / 83.46 / 82.58)

results.claim: KL reduction on hashed n-gram features correlates with average downstream F1 across 8 selection methods.
results.setup: distribution parameters estimated from 100k samples per dataset; continued pretraining setting
results.quote: The average downstream F1 score is highly correlated with the KL reduction (Pearson r = 0.82).

results.claim: Heuristic classification scores 0.5% below random selection on GLUE, which the authors attribute to the Pile already being heuristically filtered.
results.setup: same from-scratch BERT-base setup, target Wikipedia + books
results.quote: Heuristic classification leads to 0.5% lower accuracy than random selection from The Pile.
results.table: Table 3, row Heuristic classification, column Avg

results.claim: Importance resampling beats top-k selection by 0.8-0.9% GLUE average.
results.setup: from-scratch BERT-base; top-k heuristic 81.47, top-k DSIR 81.38
results.quote: DSIR without top-k is competitive with these variants on all datasets and achieves a 0.8–0.9% higher average over top-k variants.

results.claim: Generative (n-gram) importance weights beat discriminative estimators in DSIR; unigram features score 0.26% below n-grams.
results.setup: continued pretraining Table 2: fasttext discriminative 83.15, n-gram discriminative 83.19, unigram generative 83.50
results.quote: This approach (DSIR (fasttext discriminative)) improves F1 by 0.3% over heuristic classification.
results.table: Table 2, row DSIR (n-gram generative) vs DSIR (fasttext discriminative), column Avg

results.claim: Using the worst-matched pretraining set for a downstream task costs 6% F1 on average, 30% on HyperPartisan in the worst case.
results.setup: all 8x8 pairs of DSIR-selected pretraining data and downstream tasks
results.quote: We find a 6% average drop in F1 when we choose the worst pairing for each downstream task instead of matching the pretraining and downstream data.

results.claim: Within-domain transfer F1 is 82.9 versus 81.2 cross-domain.
results.setup: off-diagonal pairs of DSIR-selected data, same domain vs different domain
results.quote: We find that the within-domain F1 (82.9%) is 1.7% higher on average than the cross-domain F1 (81.2%)

results.claim: DSIR with neural (sentence-embedding GMM) features scores 81.40 GLUE, 1-1.5% over random but below n-gram DSIR.
results.quote: On average, DSIR with neural features improves by 1-1.5%+ over random selection and heuristic classification
results.table: Table 4, row DSIR + Neural features, column Avg

results.claim: Continued pretraining from BERT-base on DSIR data averages 83.99 GLUE versus 83.59 random and 83.43 for BERT-base alone.
results.setup: target formal text; continued from public BERT-base for 26B tokens
results.quote: DSIR improves over random selection by 0.4% and over BERT-base by 0.6%, achieving almost 84% on the GLUE dev set.

results.claim: In a coin-flip simulation DSIR converges to the fair target with raw data size while top-k picks all tails.
results.setup: k=10 from biased coin (0.9 heads), raw n in {100, 200, 500}
results.quote: For raw data sizes n∈{100,200,500}, DSIR selects a dataset with (44%, 47%, 50%) heads respectively, averaged over 1000 trials.

limits: n-grams capture only superficial word-level overlap; neural features could capture semantics but a preliminary version did not beat n-grams (Section 9).
The target distribution is a heuristic: Wikipedia and books as a proxy for high quality text; other targets for general-domain LMs left to future work.
Domain-specific experiments use unlabeled downstream task inputs as the target, a controlled setting; target choice matters (6% average F1 drop for the worst pairing).
Models are small (BERT-base, RoBERTa-base) masked LMs evaluated by fine-tuning; no decoder-only or large-scale LM results.
Heuristic classification losing to random is attributed to the Pile already being filtered that way (a hypothesis, not tested).
Original DAPT corpora were partly unavailable (internal S2ORC), so KL reduction for manual curation uses public approximations; DAPT checkpoints themselves are the originals.
DSIR needed a lower learning rate (8e-4) than other methods in from-scratch training since 1e-3 diverged; DSIR could amplify biases in the target data.

terms.definition: train a binary classifier to discriminate formal text from web data and select web examples with predicted probability above a noisy (Pareto) threshold
a data metric that measures how much a selected dataset reduces the KL divergence to the target (in some feature space) over random selection
